entry.title: Explore how LLNL researchers are helping shape the future of autonomous science

media:group.media:title: Explore how LLNL researchers are helping shape the future of autonomous science
media:group.media:description:
Super intelligence is increasingly being integrated into the physical world of science. At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, autonomous laboratories combine SI, robotics and automated equipment to make materials, conduct experiments, analyze results and help determine what to test next. Hear from scientists working on the cutting edge of using autonomous laboratories for materials discovery, advanced manufacturing and national security missions.

media:group.media:title: Big Ideas Lab | Tsunami Forecasting
media:group.media:description:
Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory are proving that it is possible to design a tsunami warning system that can deliver both accuracy and speed. The multi-pronged solution rides on the enormous exascale computing power of LLNL’s El Capitan supercomputer along with physics-based modeling and digital twin technologies in a collaborative effort.
Guests featured (in order of appearance):
Tzanio Kolev, Computational Mathematician, LLNL Bronis R. de Supinski, Chief Technology Officer of Livermore Computing, LLNL

media:group.media:title: Big Ideas Lab | Exoplanets
media:group.media:description:
The nearest exoplanet is about 4 light-years away, but from a single speck of light, scientists can peer into their atmospheres - and recreate pieces of these distant worlds here on Earth.
Exoplanets are planets that exist beyond our solar system, and some of them are so extreme that they challenge our understanding of how planets formed. At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, scientists are studying them in a variety of ways - two of them are: recreating the crushing pressures and temperatures of planetary interiors with powerful lasers, and developing imaging technology to detect their faint light across vast distances. Together, these approaches help reveal how distant planets form, what they’re made of, and what conditions might make them habitable.
Guests featured (in order of appearance):
Federica Coppari - Research Scientist at LLNL Benjamin Gerard - Research Scientist at LLNL
Apple: https://livermorelab.info/4B5LH2F Spotify: https://livermorelab.info/3WoUug4

entry.title: Big Ideas Lab | Rare Earth Elements

media:group.media:title: Big Ideas Lab | Rare Earth Elements
media:group.media:description:
Rare-earth elements are hidden inside nearly every piece of modern technology - your phone, electric vehicles, fighter jets. They aren't scarce in number. They're scarce because pulling them apart is one of the hardest problems in chemistry, and the United States depends almost entirely on other countries to do it.
At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, scientists are borrowing a solution nature spent millions of years perfecting - and inventing new materials that could make overlooked elements suddenly valuable - to rebuild a domestic supply chain from the ground up.
Guests featured (in order of appearance):
Scott McCall - Materials Physicist and Emeritus Actinide and Lanthanide Science Group Leader, LLNL Dan Park - Synthetic Biology Group Leader, Biosciences and Biotechnology Division, LLNL
Spotify: https://livermorelab.info/4rG56mC Apple: https://livermorelab.info/4hPhKw9

media:group.media:title: Big Ideas Lab | CODA Telescope
media:group.media:description:
The breakthrough wasn’t a new telescope. It was a new way to build one.
For decades, space telescopes were built as exquisite, one-of-a-kind instruments. Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory took a different approach: design for “good enough” instead of perfect, and rethink how a telescope is manufactured, engineered and integrated for space.
The result was CODA, an easily manufacturable, lower-cost telescope that helped turn a small NASA exoplanet mission called Pandora from an idea into something that could actually reach space.
This is what becomes possible when innovation gets crafty with the technology that’s already here.
Guests featured (in order of appearance):
Jordan Karburn - Deputy Project Manager of Pandora and Principal Investigator of the CODA Telescope, LLNL Shawn Higbee - Mission Manager for Space Sensing, LLNL
Spotify: https://livermorelab.info/4z9oURW Apple: https://livermorelab.info/46uS15M

entry.title: Big Ideas Lab | Science of Scale-Up

media:group.media:title: Big Ideas Lab | Science of Scale-Up
media:group.media:description:
A scientific breakthrough is only the beginning.
World-changing technologies can take decades to move from a successful experiment to something people can actually use. In this episode, Lawrence Livermore researchers explain the science of scale-up. From durability, cost, manufacturing, and unexpected changes in performance to the risks that can stall a promising idea, LLNL combines modeling, experimentation, risk assessment, and industry partnerships to help breakthroughs reach the real world faster and more reliably.
Guests featured (in order of appearance):
Sarah Baker - Group and Program Leader for Carbon Technologies, LLNL Andrew Wong - Materials Scientist, LLNL
Spotify: https://livermorelab.info/4iWsgms Apple: https://livermorelab.info/4wZ9fCU

media:group.media:title: Big Ideas Lab | NIF Diagnostics
media:group.media:description:
Inside the National Ignition Facility, scientists create bursts of fusion hotter than the center of the sun that vanish in 100 trillionths of a second. The only way to trust what happened is to measure it - and Lawrence Livermore has spent decades building the instruments that can see the unseeable, the same instruments that proved the world's first fusion ignition was real.
This is the story of NIF's diagnostics: how Lawrence Livermore learned to photograph a dying star, prove a nuclear stockpile still works without ever testing it, and turn an event too fast, too hot, and too dense to touch into knowledge.
Guests featured (in order of appearance):
Dave Schlossberg - Experimental Physicist, National Ignition Facility, LLNL Cara Vennari - Experimental Physicist, LLNL
Apple: https://livermorelab.info/4xerdTe Spotify: https://livermorelab.info/4wF0duO

media:group.media:title: Big Ideas Lab | STARMOC
media:group.media:description:
The number of objects in orbit is doubling every two years, and the systems built to keep watch still run on formats designed around 1960s punch cards. At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, a mission operations center called STARMOC is proving that the future of space operations can be built fast, affordable and in-house - by testing new ways to fly satellites, train AI and stay ahead in a crowded, contested sky.
This is STARMOC at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.
Guests featured (in order of appearance):
Luc Peterson - Associate Program Leader for Data Science, Space Program, LLNL Phillip Rittmuller - Principal Investigator for STARMOC
Apple: https://livermorelab.info/45aPtJw Spotify: https://livermorelab.info/4bTJ9tJ

entry.title: We Just Built a Record-Breaking Tsunami Simulation

media:group.media:title: We Just Built a Record-Breaking Tsunami Simulation
media:group.media:description:
Triggered by high-magnitude earthquakes, tsunami waves can devastate coastal regions. Some areas are overdue for a large earthquake like the Cascadia Subduction Zone in the Pacific Northwest. The challenge is predicting when a tsunami is advancing, giving communities early enough warning to respond.
Lawrence Livermore researchers and their collaborators at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of California San Diego came up with a tsunami prediction framework that combines seafloor sensor data with detailed simulations of wave behavior.
They ran the model on the exascale El Capitan supercomputer during its open science phase and used the Livermore-developed MFEM discretization software to handle the massive mathematical workload. This digital twin framework forecasts tsunami impacts in near real time! Check out Science & Technology Review to find out more.
https://str.llnl.gov/str-june-2026/tsunami-forecasting-goes-exascale

entry.title: Inside LLNL’s High Energy Density Science Internships

media:group.media:title: Inside LLNL’s High Energy Density Science Internships
media:group.media:description:
Each summer, students from across the country join Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to contribute to cutting-edge high energy density science (HEDS) research. In this video, interns share what it is like to work alongside world-class scientists and engineers, on projects ranging from theory and simulation to experiments, diagnostics, and data analysis.
Hear how these opportunities help students build technical skills, connect with mentors, and explore careers in fusion energy, materials science, and computational physics. Whether in the lab, on supercomputers, or at the experimental facility, LLNL HEDS internships offer a unique chance to learn, collaborate, and make meaningful contributions to important science.
Learn more about student opportunities by visiting LLNL’s HEDS Center website: https://heds-center.llnl.gov/join-us/student-internships
LLNL-VIDEO-2020611

media:group.media:title: Tracing Nuclear Materials at CAMS
media:group.media:description:
At the Center for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (CAMS) at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, researchers are pushing the limits of nuclear forensic science with ultra-sensitive isotope measurements. This video highlights how CAMS helps trace the origins of nuclear materials, with additional applications ranging from Earth science to cosmochemistry.
Learn more about CAMS forensic science research by visiting the CAMS website: https://cams.llnl.gov/research/forensic-science-environmental-monitoring
